title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Every clock in the catalogue models the mean beta at a set of sites and returns one number. That is not the only thing a methylation matrix can be asked, and on the field’s own evidence it may not be the most informative thing.
Tong et al. [65] quantified how much of a clock is entropy rather than biology: roughly 66 to 75 per cent of Horvath2013’s accuracy against chronological age is reproducible by a purely stochastic model of methylation change, about 90 per cent for Zhang, and about 63 per cent for PhenoAge. The gradient is the interesting part. The more accurately a clock predicts chronological age, the more of it is drift.
This page covers five things FALCONAge computes that are not clocks: the disorder readouts, repertoire structure, where a clock’s coefficient mass sits, reliability components, and mosaic ages within a tissue. None of them returns an age, none is gated by scale_type, and none is comparable between datasets processed differently.

title: Beyond the clock score
section: Disorder: entropy, drift and the barometer
text:
Disorder: entropy, drift and the barometer
falconage.disorder holds four functions, and the division between them is about what carries the number, which is the distinction most easily lost.








Function
Returns
Per what




fa.entropy
how far the methylome sits from fully committed
sample


fa.drift
how far a sample sits from the cohort centroid
sample


fa.noise_barometer
summed per-site SD over age-variable sites
group


fa.variable_sites
which cytosines widen with age
site




Entropy
Normalised Shannon entropy over the beta matrix:
\[
S = \frac{1}{N \log \tfrac{1}{2}} \sum_{i=1}^{N}
    \Big[ \beta_i \log \beta_i + (1-\beta_i) \log (1-\beta_i) \Big]
\]
Bounded 0 to 1. A site at beta 0 or 1 is decided and contributes nothing; a site at 0.5 is maximally uncertain and contributes its full share. So \(S = 0\) is a methylome where every site is committed and \(S = 1\) is one where none of them is.
import falconage as fa

data = fa.read("betas.csv")
ent = fa.entropy(data)        # entropy, n_sites
n_sites is not decoration. Entropy is a mean over sites, so a mean over different sites is not a comparison. The default restricts to sites covered in every sample for exactly that reason; set complete_sites=False to use each sample’s own coverage and then read n_sites before comparing any two rows.
On the test corpus this lands at 0.695 with an SD of 0.007 across 825,177 complete sites, which is what a clean bimodal EPIC distribution looks like once it is summarised to one number.


Drift
The barometer is a property of a group, which leaves nothing to regress against an outcome. fa.drift is the per-sample analogue: the distance from the cohort centroid, computed leave-one-out so that a sample is never scored against a mean it helped compute.
dri = fa.drift(data)                          # drift from this cohort
dri = fa.drift(data, reference=young_mean)    # drift from a young reference
The leave-one-out default matters more than it looks. Scoring a sample against a centroid that includes it shrinks its own distance, and in a small cohort that shrinkage is large enough to invert a group difference.


Which sites actually widen
The barometer of Mei et al. [70] is defined over “cytosines whose variance rises with age”, and that clause is the whole statistic. Summed over every site instead, the sum is dominated by sites that are merely variable, most of which have nothing to do with age.
fa.variable_sites is that selection step, split out so it can be inspected rather than assumed. The test is Brown-Forsythe, which is Levene’s test using the median, across age bins. Bartlett’s test is the more common choice in this literature and is the wrong one here: it assumes normality within each group, and beta values near 0 or 1 are visibly not normal, so Bartlett reports variance differences that are distributional artefacts.
A significant result says the variances differ between bins. It does not say variance rises, and a site whose variance falls is just as significant, so direction carries the sign of the trend and rising is the conjunction the barometer wants.






ImportantWhat this looks like on a cohort that is too small



Run on the test corpus, sites_rising under Benjamini-Hochberg is zero. Twenty-seven samples in three bins of nine, against roughly 820,000 tests, has almost no power once the correction is applied.
That is the correct answer, not a gap in the implementation. A barometer that means anything needs a cohort in the hundreds. fa.noise_barometer accepts an explicit sites= list so a selection made elsewhere can be reused, which is also the only way the statistic transfers between cohorts.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Repertoire structure
falconage.immune addresses a covariate no published blood clock carries.
Deconvolution answers how many cells of each type. It says nothing about how many distinct clones those cells represent, and the two are different measurements: two donors with an identical CD8 memory fraction can differ by orders of magnitude in clone count.

Why clone count should move a clock at all
Take one cell type holding fraction \(f\) of the sample, split into clones of relative size \(w_k\) with \(\sum_k w_k = 1\). Give clone \(k\) a somatic offset \(\delta_k\) from its lineage mean at some site, with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\). The compartment’s bulk beta is the size-weighted mean, so
\[
\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_k w_k \delta_k\Big] = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2
   = \frac{\sigma^2}{N_{\text{eff}}},
\qquad N_{\text{eff}} = \Big(\sum_k w_k^2\Big)^{-1}
\]
and \(\sum_k w_k^2\) is exactly the Simpson index. The variance a clonal compartment contributes to bulk methylation is inversely proportional to its effective number of clones, and clone count enters through that quantity and no other. Three equal clones carry one cell’s somatic state at full weight; ten thousand clones average it to nothing.
This is why the effect is invisible to composition adjustment: \(f\) can be identical between two donors while \(N_{\text{eff}}\) differs thousand-fold, and every published blood clock sees only \(f\).
The myeloid version of the question is settled. Nachun et al. [71] measured clonal hematopoiesis against six clocks and found 1.31 years of acceleration on GrimAge to 3.08 on extrinsic EEAA. The lymphoid analogue has not been asked.


Measuring it
div = fa.repertoire_diversity(clones, sample_col="sample_id", count_col="count")
data.obs = data.obs.join(div)

res = fa.score(data, clocks="compatible")
acc = fa.acceleration(res, adjust=["clonality", "cd8mem_fraction"])
fa.acceleration already accepts arbitrary obs columns as covariates, so the incremental test is one call. The question is entirely whether clonality adds variance beyond cell fraction.
Depth is the trap. Richness and Shannon both rise with sequencing depth, so an unrarefied comparison between a deeply and a shallowly sequenced donor measures the library rather than the donor. Pass rarefy="min" to subsample every donor to a common depth by multivariate hypergeometric draw, which is what a shallower run would actually have produced; sampling with replacement inflates richness at low depth, in the same direction as the bias being corrected. clonality, simpson and effective_clones are far more stable and are the ones to trust when rarefaction is not possible.


Simulating it
The mechanism arm needs no paired cohort. fa.simulate_clonality generates bulk methylomes at fixed cell fractions and varying clone structure, so anything a clock does in response is clone structure alone.
sim = fa.simulate_clonality(
    reference, {"CD8mem": 0.3, "Neu": 0.7},
    clonal_types=["CD8mem"],
    clone_sizes=[fa.immune.zipf_clone_sizes(n, alpha=1.0)
                 for n in (2, 20, 200, 2000)],
    n_replicates=20)
res = fa.score(sim, clocks="compatible")
reference is sorted-cell mean beta, features by cell type. The six-cell IDOL library that the bundled deconvolution entries use (FlowSorted.Blood.EPIC, GPL-3) is one such table: fa.registry.load().deconvolution_table("deconvolutebloodepicbcell", "EPICv1") returns it, 450 CpGs by six cell types.






NoteWhat the simulation returns on the test corpus



Across 42 clocks scored on 48 simulated samples at identical cell fractions, the median log-log slope of score spread against effective clone count is -0.494, interquartile range -0.559 to -0.415. The derivation predicts -0.5 and was not fitted to the simulation.
Among the clocks reporting years, dnamphenoage moves 4.35 years between an effectively-two-clone compartment and a diverse one, and horvath2013 moves 1.54 years. Both fall below a year once the compartment holds a few hundred effective clones.
Cell-type fractions were identical for every one of those samples, so composition adjustment cannot remove any of it.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Where a clock’s weight sits
A clock is a weight vector over CpGs, and two questions about that vector need no samples at all.
Is this clock exposed to genotype? If a clock CpG is under strong meQTL control and the allele frequency at that variant differs between ancestral populations, a systematic difference in clock output between ancestry groups follows from genotype frequency alone, with no difference in aging. Cruz-Gonzalez et al. [75] established that the major clocks lose accuracy in admixed individuals; whether the size of that loss tracks each clock’s meQTL exposure is open, and half of that measurement is a property of the coefficients.
Is this clock regulatory? Patel et al. [76] report that most CpGs used by established clocks do not overlap known transcription factor binding sites. Reproducing that against any annotation class is the same computation with a different list.
mass = fa.coefficient_mass({"meqtl": godmc_cpgs, "enhancer": enhancer_cpgs})

Why mass and not count
Counting annotated sites answers the wrong question. A clock’s behaviour is driven by its heavy features: a 353-CpG clock with two enormous weights and 351 small ones behaves like a two-CpG clock. The statistic is therefore the share of \(\sum_j |w_j|\) on annotated sites, with the plain count returned beside it. When the two diverge, the annotated sites are the heavy ones, and that divergence is the finding.
Run on the registry with each clock’s own CpG set as the annotation, which needs no external file, horvath2013 shares 11.6 per cent of its sites with dnamphenoage but 19.6 per cent of its mass. weidner shares two of its three sites with dnamphenoage and 89 per cent of its mass. Two clocks that share their heaviest features will agree with each other for reasons that have nothing to do with either being right.
FALCONAge bundles no annotation list. meQTL catalogues and regulatory builds are large, versioned and separately licensed, and freezing one into a wheel would make it silently stale. GoDMC and the EPIGEN meQTL database are the usual sources for the first question, the Ensembl Regulatory Build or a Roadmap chromatin-state track for the second. .attrs["unmatched"] reports how many supplied ids matched nothing, which is the check that catches an EPIC v2 list with _TC21 suffixes meeting bare cg probe ids.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Reliability: trait, state and technical
A published ICC answers “how reproducible is this clock across a cohort”. Someone asking “has my number moved” needs a different quantity, and the gap between the two is why clock ICCs in the literature read as reassuring while replicate disagreement of up to nine years is also true [68].
fa.variance_components separates them, given repeated measurement:
\[
y_{ijk} = \mu + a_i + s_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}
\]
for person \(i\), occasion \(j\), replicate \(k\), fitted by Henderson’s method of moments. Two ICCs come back and the gap between them is the point:

icc

On raw scores. Comparable to what the literature publishes.

icc_age_adjusted

The same after chronological age is regressed out. A cohort spanning decades holds most of its between-person variance in the age term, so a raw ICC largely reports that the clock tracks age, which was never in question. The adjusted figure is between-person reliability among people of the same age, which is what any individual-level claim rests on.


A clock whose raw ICC is 0.98 and whose adjusted ICC is 0.4 is not a precise instrument. It is a cohort with a wide age range.
vc = fa.variance_components(res, subject_col="donor", occasion_col="visit")
vc.table                      # var_trait, var_state, var_tech, icc, icc_age_adjusted
vc.replicates_needed(0.9)     # per occasion, to reach ICC 0.9
With one draw per visit and no technical replicates, which is the usual longitudinal design, day-to-day change and assay noise cannot be told apart: var_state then holds both, var_tech is NaN, icc is the test-retest reliability across visits, and vc.design["within_person"] says so.
replicates_needed returns inf where no number of replicates gets there, and that is the informative case rather than an error. Replicates average away the technical term only, so a clock whose day-to-day within-person variance already exceeds the budget cannot be rescued by running the array again. The honest answer is then a second draw, not a second scan.
Components are not clipped at zero. A negative one means the within-level spread exceeded the between-level spread, which is real for a small design or a clock measuring nothing in this cohort, and rounding it to zero disguises both.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Mosaic ages within a tissue
fa.models.single_cell.scage gives an age per cell [28]. A bulk clock already reports the mean, so the quantity worth having is the shape of the distribution underneath it: a tissue whose cells are uniformly middle-aged and one holding a mixture of young and very old cells have the same bulk methylation and, plausibly, very different biology.
The obstacle is that single-cell methylation coverage is sparse, so each per-cell age rests on few sites and carries large error. Observed spread is therefore always positive, and reporting it as heterogeneity is the mistake fa.mosaic exists to avoid.
The null is stated plainly: every cell in the group has the same true age, and all observed spread is estimation error. It is simulated by drawing each cell from a normal centred on the group mean with that cell’s own standard error, taken from the profile-likelihood width scage already returns.
ages = fa.models.single_cell.scage(cells, reference)
mos  = fa.mosaic(ages, group="tissue")
A small p_excess is evidence of genuine mosaicism. A large one says the data cannot distinguish a mosaic tissue from a uniform one measured badly, which at typical single-cell coverage is the usual answer and is worth reporting as such. n_at_grid_edge counts cells whose estimate landed on the boundary of the age grid, where the likelihood was truncated rather than maximised; those pile up and inflate the tails, so a group with many of them should have its skew and kurtosis ignored.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
What none of this is
None of these functions is a clock, and none returns an age. They carry no coefficients, no scale_type gate applies, and their outputs move with normalisation, probe panel and detection-p filtering. The only defensible comparison is within one processed matrix.
That is a real constraint rather than a disclaimer. Entropy computed on noob-normalised betas and entropy computed on raw betas are different numbers for the same DNA, and neither is more correct than the other.

title: Age acceleration
text:
The conventions disagree by several years on the same data, and papers frequently do not say which they used.

PythonR


fa.acceleration(res, method="absolute")      # predicted - chronological
fa.acceleration(res, method="residual")      # residual of predicted on chronological
fa.acceleration(res, method="both")          # both, as <clock>_absolute / <clock>_residual
fa.acceleration(res, method="within_group", group="dataset")


acceleration(res, method = "absolute")
acceleration(res, method = "residual")
acceleration(res, method = "both")
acceleration(res, method = "within_group", group = "dataset")



Absolute is interpretable in years and carries the clock’s own bias: a clock five years high on everybody gives everybody five years of acceleration. Residual removes that bias, and removes any real cohort-wide effect with it. Within-group is what the AA2 benchmark needs: it asks whether cases accelerate relative to their own controls. "both" returns the first two side by side, suffixed, for when you would otherwise have to pick without knowing which the comparison paper used.


The residual is centred on this cohort, so it cannot say how the cohort compares with anyone else, and it absorbs any effect the whole cohort shares. method="reference" fits the age line in a second, scored population and applies it unchanged here:
ref = fa.score(reference_data, clocks=["phenoage"])
fa.acceleration(res, method="reference", reference=ref, match=("age", "sex"))
The line is fitted separately within each level of the categorical match columns (usually sex), an age outside the reference’s range in its stratum is refused rather than extrapolated, and a reference scored with different coefficients is refused. attrs["reference_fit"] records, per clock and stratum, the reference sample size, age range, fitted line and residual SD.



Blood cell composition changes with age, and with most other things that happen to a person. In more than 10,000 blood samples, immune composition was significantly associated with age acceleration for every one of six widely used clocks (Zhang et al., Aging Cell 2024;23:e14071, doi:10.1111/acel.14071), so an unadjusted acceleration is measuring two things and reporting one number.
The proportions needed to separate them are usually already in the result, computed by the deconvolution clocks in the same run:

PythonR


fa.cell_composition(res)                        # the proportions, as covariates
fa.acceleration(res, adjust="cell_composition") # net of them
fa.acceleration(res, adjust=["cd8t", "mono"])   # or measured counts from obs


cell_composition(res)
acceleration(res, adjust = "cell_composition")
acceleration(res, adjust = c("cd8t", "mono"))



An adjusted acceleration is a different quantity from an unadjusted one, so the returned frame records which covariates went in. Comparing the two as though they were the same measurement is the error this is designed to make visible.
Ask for acceleration on a pace-of-aging clock and it refuses:

IllegalOperationError: 'acceleration' is not defined for dunedinpoam38, whose output is
  pace_ratio (biological years per chronological year).
  Legal here: correlate, difference, mean, rank.
  A pace of aging is already a rate; subtracting chronological age from it is a units
  error, not a conservative choice.

That refusal is the point. A wrong number in a column of numbers is invisible.

title: Age acceleration
section: 9. Downstream statistics on an aging score
text:
9. Downstream statistics on an aging score

9.1 Association with chronological age
Pearson r, Spearman ρ, MAE, MedAE, RMSE, and the regression slope of BA on CA. The slope is the diagnostic: penalised regression compresses predictions toward the training mean, so slopes < 1 are normal and produce the well-documented systematic underestimation in older subjects. Report the slope, not just r.


9.2 Mortality
Cox proportional hazards with the standardised score plus CA and sex as covariates:
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ scale(BA_advance) + age + gender, data)
Report the HR per SD with 95% CI. BioAge standardises the advance within sex so the effect size means “one sex-specific SD of biological age advancement” (BioAge table_surv.R). Observed HRs from BioAge’s NHANES IV tables run 1.21–1.61 per SD across measures and subgroups, with KDM advance, PhenoAge advance and homeostatic dysregulation broadly comparable (BioAge README).
Additional model families worth supporting: time-dependent ROC/AUC, Harrell’s C-index, competing risks (Fine–Gray), and SuperLearner ensembles with out-of-fold predictions (the TwinGene/UK Biobank pipeline uses 10-fold CV, optionally repeated across seeds).


9.3 Morbidity and phenotype
Logistic or Poisson models for prevalent and incident disease; multimorbidity counts; frailty index; intrinsic capacity; grip strength and gait speed; cognitive scores. Interaction tests for BA × (BMI, sex, smoking, education) are standard in the epidemiological literature.


9.4 Group comparison and intervention response
The ComputAgeBench formulation, which is the cleanest published statement of the problem (ComputAge benchmarking.py:339–397):

AA2 - is the age acceleration in an aging-accelerating condition (AAC) cohort greater than in healthy controls from the same study? One-sided Welch’s t-test if Δ is assumed normal, else one-sided Mann–Whitney U.
AA1 - is the age acceleration in an AAC cohort greater than zero, with no control group? One-sided one-sample t-test, else one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank.
Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction is applied per model across datasets, then thresholded at 0.05.

For paired intervention designs, use paired tests on within-subject deltas and report both the absolute change and the change relative to the measurement’s own ICC.


9.5 Reliability
Intraclass correlation coefficient on technical replicates (same DNA, two arrays) and on biological replicates (same person, short interval). Pool across studies with Fisher-Z. The result to remember is from Sehgal et al. (bioRxiv 2025.10.13.682176), on the TranslAGE platform: technical reproducibility does not predict biological reliability, and PCGrimAge was the only clock reaching ICC > 0.75 for biological reliability. A tool should surface each clock’s published ICC next to its prediction.

title: Figures and reports
text:
Two documents, each one self-contained HTML file.
The one-page report is the scores, the run and a few figures, small enough to send:
write_results(res, "results/")
report(res, "report.html", group = "condition")
It is one file, inlined CSS, base64 figures, the table embedded, so it still works after somebody emails it, which is the only thing anybody does with a report.
The full run, step by step. run_report() runs quality control, scoring, technical error, prediction intervals, age acceleration, a consensus test across clocks when a group column is named, and the interpretation tables, and writes every deliverable into one directory: the same directory the report command writes. With quarto = TRUE it adds falconage_report.qmd, in which every file of that directory sits under the step that produced it, in the order a reader has to take them, because each step is only as reliable as the ones before it:







Step
What it holds




0. Provenance
versions, the coefficient file and SHA-256 behind each clock, device, warnings


1. Input and quality control
per-sample missingness and beta distribution; the QC figures


2. Coverage
per-clock coverage by feature count and by coefficient weight; clocks not scored, and why


3. Scores
the scores, what each category of clock measures, and how the clocks relate


4. Agreement with chronological age
error against age and whether it depends on age


5. Uncertainty
technical standard error and conformal prediction intervals


6. Age acceleration
residuals on age, for the scales where they are defined


7. Group comparison
the consensus verdict and the test for every clock


8. Interpretation
what each score means and the published evidence, with DOIs


9. Further outputs
every other file in the directory, named and sized



A file the report does not recognise still appears, in step 9, so nothing in the directory is left out. Tables expand, search, page and download as CSV; figures enlarge on click and download at full resolution. Rendered, it is one HTML file with every figure and table embedded: 3.7 MB for 16 samples and three clocks.

PythonRCommand line


fa.report.run_report(d, "results/", group_col="condition", quarto=True)


run_report(d, "results/", group = "condition", quarto = TRUE)


docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu \
  report betas.csv --outdir results/ --group-col condition --quarto



Rendering it. Quarto is not in the FALCONAge image. Installed it takes 423 MB, which would add about 17% to the 2.5 GB image for an optional document, so inside the image the source is written and the run says so. Render it with the Quarto container, from the output directory, and open falconage_report.html:
cd results
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w \
  ghcr.io/quarto-dev/quarto quarto render falconage_report.qmd
Where Quarto is installed, run_report() renders it directly, and quarto_report("results/") (R) or fa.report.write_quarto_report("results/", render=True) (Python) rewrites the report for a directory that already exists.

title: Figures and reports
text:
10. Plots

10.1 The standard set

BA vs CA scatter, faceted by clock, coloured by sex, with a fitted line, the identity line, and Pearson r annotated in the corner. This is plot_ba (BioAge plot_ba.R), ggplot2, geom_point(shape = 1), geom_smooth(method = lm), facet_wrap(~ method, scales = "free"), colours #7294D4 (men) and #E6A0C4 (women).
Pairs / correlation matrix of age accelerations. Scatter plots below the diagonal, Pearson r above the diagonal colour-mapped, clock labels on the diagonal. plot_baa (BioAge plot_baa.R) implements this in base graphics with a custom layout() matrix so the diagonal cells can hold text.
Hierarchical clustering + Spearman heatmap of clocks. pyaging Figure 1a - 38 methylation clocks over ~13,000 samples; telomere predictors cluster together, chronological predictors separate from mortality predictors.
UMAP of samples in clock space. pyaging Figures 1b–e; reveals “ageotypes” where AltumAge (chronological) and GrimAge2 (mortality) disagree.
Reprogramming / intervention timecourse. pyaging Figure 1f, GSE54848, 39 clocks over OSKM days; most rejuvenate between days 10 and 20, telomere predictors go up, ENCen100 is flat. Any tool should make “run N clocks across a timepoint variable and plot trajectories” a one-liner.
Benchmark grids. ComputAgeBench plot_class_bench - a boolean matrix of clock × (dataset:condition:test) with per-condition-class column groups and a total column; plot_medae (MedAE bar chart, upper bound 18 y); plot_bias (median error, x-limits ±20 y). Saved as PDF at 180 dpi (ComputAge benchmarking.py:451).
Forest plot of hazard ratios per clock, per outcome, per cohort.
Density / violin of age acceleration by group (disease vs control, treated vs untreated).
Organ or system radar/heatmap. organAging uses heatmaps of organ ages against traits, medications, foods, professions, diseases; SystemsAge gives an 11-spoke profile.
Expression-density QC plots at each preprocessing stage. tAge’s plot_eset_density is called after raw, RLE, log, scale, YuGene and centring - a cheap way to catch a broken normalisation.
Volcano / GSEA plots when linking clock features to biology.
Spatial maps of predicted age or age acceleration over tissue coordinates, plus proximity effect matrices (effector cell type × target cell type, coloured by t-statistic).
Calibration plot for probability-output clocks; precision–recall curve for classifiers on imbalanced test sets (CellBiAge’s choice of AUPRC over AUROC).
Missingness bar chart per clock, percent of features absent, drawn before the results so the user sees which clocks are untrustworthy for their platform.



10.2 Plotting conventions worth adopting

Always draw the identity line on BA-vs-CA plots.
Never plot rate clocks (DunedinPACE) on the same axis as age clocks.
Facet by clock generation, not alphabetically.
Annotate every panel with n, r and the missingness fraction.
Colour by group, shape by platform; keep the palette stable across the whole report.



10.3 What FALCONAge draws, and against which of the above
Thirty-one figures in Python, twenty of them also in R, drawn alike because both languages read their colours, titles, subtitles and one-line descriptions from the same colorscheme.yaml. The table lists those that answer the principles above; the gallery shows every one. Every function returns its data frame as well as its figure, which is how two rendering engines draw the same numbers.

title: Benchmarking and validation
text:
11. Benchmarking and validation

11.1 ComputAgeBench, the reference methodology



The two tests, and why the one without controls has its credit discounted


AA2 compares a condition group against its own healthy controls from the same study, so a clock that over-predicts everybody gains nothing from it. AA1 has no controls to compare against and asks only whether the condition group’s acceleration sits above zero, which a uniformly over-predicting clock passes everywhere. The total discounts the AA1 credit by the clock’s own median signed error on healthy controls, measured on the same data, which is the correction that separates a clock that detects disease from a clock with a broken intercept.
computage (Kriukov, Efimov, Kuzmina, Khrameeva, Dylov; bioRxiv 2024.06.06.597715; KDD ’25) [36].
Premise. MAE against chronological age is the wrong metric because a perfect chronological oracle is useless. Instead, a good clock must show higher age acceleration in people with pre-defined aging-accelerating conditions (AACs) than in healthy controls.
Data. Benchmark split: 10,404 samples, 900,449 CpGs, 65 studies. Training split: 7,419 samples, 907,766 CpGs, 46 studies (healthy people only). Hosted on Hugging Face at computage/computage_bench as per-study parquet plus a single computage_bench_meta.tsv.
Condition classes (ComputAge data_utils.py):







Class
Conditions




HC
healthy control


CVD
AS (atherosclerosis), IHD, CVA (stroke)


ISD
IBD, HIV, HIV_TB


MBD
XOB (extreme obesity), T1D, T2D


MSD
OP (osteoporosis), RA


NDD
MS, PD, AD, CJD


RSD
TB, COPD


PGS
CGL (congenital generalised lipodystrophy), WS (Werner), HGPS (progeria)



The full study table with GSE accessions, PMIDs, first authors, tissues, sample counts and HC availability is ComputAge BenchBSB_table.csv - 66 rows. Highlights: GSE56046 (n = 1,202, atherosclerosis), GSE42861 (n = 689, RA), GSE117859 (n = 608, HIV), GSE111629 (n = 572, PD), GSE59685 (n = 531, AD), GSE131752 (Werner, n = 48), GSE182991 (HGPS, n = 27), GSE214297 (CGL, n = 16).
Filters. Tissues restricted to Blood, Saliva, Buccal (“BSB”). Age limited to [18, 90], except progeria (PGS) which is exempt so that young progeria patients are retained.
Scoring.
AA2_score = number of AA2 datasets where FDR-adjusted p < 0.05
AA1_score = number of AA1 datasets where FDR-adjusted p < 0.05
MedAE     = median |prediction − age| over all healthy-control samples
MedE      = median (prediction − age) over healthy controls          # the bias
total     = AA2_score + AA1_score × (1 − max(0, MedE) / MedAE)
The bias penalty is the clever part: a clock that simply over-predicts everyone’s age will pass AA1 trivially, so AA1 credit is discounted by how much of the clock’s error is systematic positive bias (ComputAge benchmarking.py:427). GrimAge2 leads AA1 but carries a large positive HC bias, which the formula penalises.
Running it. ComputAge’s run_benchmark(models_config, experiment_prefix, output_folder), not fa.run_benchmark, where models_config has an in_library dict (clock name → params, notably imputation) and a new_models dict (name → path to a pickled sklearn estimator with feature_names_in_). Outputs: AA2 and AA1 p-value CSVs, FDR-corrected boolean CSVs, MedAE CSV, bias CSV, four PDFs, and a pickled benchmark object.


11.2 Biolearn and the Biomarkers of Aging Consortium
Open-source Python library providing a unified interface over aging biomarkers plus a data library that loads GEO, NHANES and Framingham. Reference implementations for 39 biomarkers evaluated over >20,000 individuals; the framework paper reports integration of 17 additional GEO datasets covering 12,463 samples across tissues and age ranges. Version 0.7.0 released January 2025. The consortium runs a Synapse challenge series (chronological age, mortality, multimorbidity) with >$200k in prizes. ComputAge’s model_definitions are explicitly ported from biolearn (ComputAge definitions.py).


11.3 TranslAGE - reliability validation
TranslAGE (Borrus et al., bioRxiv 2025.10.16.682960) harmonises 179 blood methylation datasets and precomputes 41 biomarker scores. On it, Sehgal et al. (bioRxiv 2025.10.13.682176) measured technical and biological ICCs for 18 clocks, pooled with Fisher-Z: technical reproducibility did not predict biological reliability, PCGrimAge was the only clock with biological ICC > 0.75, and the PC-based clocks, PCGrimAge and SystemsAge in particular, stayed technically reliable across slide positions and DNA extraction protocols.


11.4 Intervention responsiveness
In CALERIE, two years of calorie restriction (about 12% below baseline intake in practice) slowed DunedinPACE by 2 to 3% against controls (Waziry et al., Nature Aging 2023, doi:10.1038/s43587-022-00357-y), the first randomised trial to move a methylation clock. Ordering: DunedinPACE responds fastest, GrimAge needs longer or larger interventions, first-generation Horvath barely moves.


11.5 What a benchmarking module in the new tool should do

Chronological accuracy on healthy controls: MedAE, MAE, RMSE, r, ρ, slope, bias (MedE).
AA1 and AA2 with configurable distributional assumption and FDR correction.
Mortality: HR per SD, C-index, time-dependent AUC.
Reliability: ICC from user-supplied replicate structure, with Fisher-Z pooling.
Responsiveness: paired-design effect sizes with the measurement ICC reported alongside.
Cross-clock agreement: Spearman matrix, hierarchical clustering, UMAP.
A composite leaderboard using the ComputAgeBench total-score formula, with the components shown, never just the total.

One row per clock: how many of its features are present, and – where the coefficients are available – how much of the model’s total weight those present features carry, plus the heaviest probes that are missing.

A count treats every probe as interchangeable, and an elastic net’s weights are nothing like uniform. “92% of probes present” covers both “the missing 8% are negligible” and “the missing 8% carry a third of the model”. How many samples to see an effect
text:
The first thing a laboratory needs, and it is needed before any array is run. Two independent groups, two-sided.


power_n(
  clock,
  effect,
  sd = NULL,
  result = NULL,
  icc = NULL,
  alpha = 0.05,
  power = 0.8,
  replicates = 1L
)




clock:
Clock name.
effect:
The difference worth detecting, in the clock’s own unit. No default: a power calculation with an assumed effect size is a way of writing down an assumption without noticing.
sd:
Population SD of the score. Measured from result when given.
result:
A scored pilot. Supplies sd, and – if technical_se() has been called on it – a measured ICC for this laboratory.
icc:
Override the reliability figure.
alpha, power:
Significance and target power.
replicates:
Assay each sample this many times and average.




A list with n_per_group, n_total, the reliability used and where it came from, and the n a perfectly repeatable assay would need.



Reliability is part of the answer: the SD a user measures already contains the assay’s noise, so splitting it out with the clock’s test-retest ICC says how much of the sample size is buying signal and how much is averaging out the instrument. That is the arithmetic behind the finding that the original clocks need 3-16 replicates per condition where their principal-component versions need 1-2.

AA2, for a dataset with controls: is the condition group’s acceleration higher than its controls’? One-sided Mann-Whitney, BH corrected.

Does a group difference hold up across clocks?
text:
Implements the decision rule from When to Trust Epigenetic Clocks (PMC11526921). Re-analysing six intervention datasets, the authors found that in five of them exactly one clock reached significance – a first-generation clock every time – and four of those five lost it under multiple-testing correction. In no case did the principal-component version of the same clock corroborate the finding. Their conclusion, stated plainly: a single significant clock after an intervention is likely a false positive.


consensus(
  x,
  group_col,
  reference = NULL,
  alpha = 0.05,
  design = "independent",
  subject_col = NULL
)




x:
A falcon_result.
group_col:
Column with exactly two levels, or with two or more visits for design = "mixed".
reference:
Which level is the comparison group.
alpha:
Significance level.
design:
"independent" (Welch’s t-test), "paired" or "mixed".
subject_col:
Column naming the person each sample came from; needed by the paired and mixed designs.




A list with verdict (supported, unsupported, inconclusive), why – which always carries the counts it was computed from – and the per-clock table.



Each clock is tested on its acceleration residual where that is a legal operation for its scale, and on the raw score where it is not. A pace of aging has no residual to take.
Repeated measurements on the same people take design = "paired" (two visits, a paired t-test on each person’s change) or design = "mixed" (two or more visits, y ~ visit + (1 | person) by REML with nlme’s containment degrees of freedom, so a person with a missed visit still counts). Both add mdc95, the minimum detectable change \1.96\SEM\ (Weir 2005, doi:10.1519/15184.1), and flag significant mean changes smaller than it.

Split conformal: the half-width is a quantile of the absolute residual on a calibration set of healthy blood samples with known ages, so on any sample exchangeable with that cohort the interval covers the truth at the stated rate, with no distributional assumption and a finite-sample guarantee.

A clock trained on 450K runs perfectly well on EPIC data that carries its probes, and fails on 450K data filtered to 20,000 probes. Only the feature list can answer whether a clock is usable, which is what compatible_clocks() checks.
But high coverage does not make a result meaningful. The mammalian methylation array was designed around CpGs conserved across mammals, and carries 96% of Horvath2013’s 353 probes - so a zebra scores at higher coverage than many human 450K datasets and returns a confident number from a clock fitted on people. Nothing in the arithmetic can notice. Set species and FALCONAge warns:

d <- falcon_data(betas, modality = "dna_methylation", species = "Equus grevyi")
res <- score(d, clocks = "horvath2013")
manifest(res)$warnings
#> trained on Homo sapiens, scored on Equus grevyi. Feature coverage says nothing
#> about whether the coefficients transfer across species.

The distinction between B and C matters. C is a licensing decision by the authors. B is an honesty one by us: copying a coefficient set out of another package without knowing where that package got it is how the known paper-versus-implementation discrepancies spread in the first place, and a traced extractor is a welcome contribution.

title: Loading your data
text:
Nine input types reach the same place: a FalconData carrying a samples-by-features matrix, the modality, the platform, and whatever sample annotation came with the file. Once you have one, scoring is the same call whatever you loaded.
Every output on this page was produced by running the code above it, against the public test corpus where the corpus has that input type and against a small file written inline where it does not. Nothing here is illustrative.

fa.read(path) dispatches on the file name when you would rather not choose. It is convenience, not magic: it says which reader it picked, and any argument that reader needs has to be passed to the reader itself.

title: Loading your data
text:
Raw Illumina IDATs
A directory of _Grn.idat and _Red.idat pairs, one pair per sample, exactly as the scanner writes them. The array manifest is fetched once and cached.
import falconage as fa

d = fa.read_idat_dir("idats/")
d = fa.prepare(d)              # noob, BMIQ, probe masks, id harmonisation
INFO    fetched ebc36febf212e1d2_HumanMethylationEPIC_manifest_v2.csv.gz (23.7 MB)
FalconData(2 samples x 865918 features, dna_methylation, EPICv1, 2.0% missing)
FalconData(2 samples x 865859 features, dna_methylation, EPICv1, 2.0% missing)
The feature count drops by 59 across prepare(): those are the probes the published masks exclude, not samples lost. Platform is detected from the manifest and the probe count rather than declared.
EPIC v2 needs one more thing, and it is automatic. Its probe ids carry a suffix (cg00000029_TC21), and a clock fitted on 450K sees zero overlap with them until the suffixes are collapsed. prepare() does that by default; aggregate_epicv2=False turns it off, and there is no good reason to.

title: Loading your data
text:
A beta matrix
Probes down the rows, samples across the columns, or the transpose: the orientation is detected from which axis carries probe ids.
d = fa.read_betas("betas.csv")
FalconData(3 samples x 3 features, dna_methylation, 0.0% missing)
The file that produced it:
probe,S001,S002,S003
cg00000029,0.512,0.488,0.559
cg00000165,0.113,0.096,0.140
cg00000236,0.842,0.871,0.836
Betas belong in 0 to 1. A matrix of percentages is a factor of a hundred out and every clock will return a confidently wrong number, so prepare() checks the range and says so.

d = fa.read_series_matrix("GSE330325_series_matrix.txt.gz")
d.obs.head(3)

title: Loading your data
text:
RRBS and bisulfite coverage
One file per sample, each a table of positions with methylated and unmethylated counts. Sites are intersected across samples and thresholded on coverage.
d = fa.read_rrbs_dir(["20D02.overlap.txt.gz", "20D03.overlap.txt.gz",
                      "M3503.overlap.txt.gz"], min_coverage=5)
FalconData(3 samples x 1976936 features, rrbs, RRBS, 1.9% missing)
Two million shared sites from three files, and the sites are genomic coordinates rather than probe ids. An array clock cannot be scored on them directly; that needs a liftover this package does not ship, and it says so rather than matching on position and hoping.

title: Loading your data
text:
Nanopore bedMethyl
modkit output, one row per site with the modification fraction in column 11.
s = fa.read_bedmethyl("sample.bed", sample_id="ONT01", min_coverage=10)
feature_id
chr1:10468    0.733
chr1:10470    0.120

Name: ONT01, dtype: float64
One file gives a Series; read_bedmethyl_dir() gives a FalconData across the sites the files share. The fraction is converted from the percentage the format stores, so what you get back is already a beta.

title: Loading your data
text:
A targeted assay
Pyrosequencing, EpiTYPER, ddPCR: a handful of CpGs measured directly, with samples down the rows.
d = fa.read_panel("panel.csv")
FalconData(2 samples x 3 features, dna_methylation, targeted panel, 0.0% missing)
sample,cg16867657,cg09809672,cg02228185
P01,0.68,0.41,0.55
P02,0.72,0.38,0.51
A panel almost never carries a whole clock, and the coverage floor is what stops a three-probe file being scored as though it were a 353-probe model. probe_loss() says what a partial set costs before you score anything.

title: Loading your data
text:
Clinical chemistry
The clinical clocks take laboratory values, and they take them in declared units.
UNITS = {"albumin": "g/L", "creatinine": "umol/L", "glucose": "mmol/L",
         "crp": "mg/L", "lymphocyte_percent": "%", "mean_cell_volume": "fL",
         "red_cell_distribution_width": "%", "alkaline_phosphatase": "U/L",
         "white_blood_cell_count": "10^9/L"}

d = fa.read_clinical("labs.csv", units=UNITS)
fa.score(d, clocks=["phenoage"]).scores.round(2)
FalconData(2 samples x 10 features, clinical_chemistry, 0.0% missing)

WARNING [phenoage] Two constants circulate in the divisor of the Gompertz inversion:
0.090165 and 0.09165. FALCONAge uses 0.090165, the value BioAge corrected to in April
2026. Code still using 0.09165 differs by several years on the same input.

           phenoage
sample_id
C01           55.79
C02           69.61
Units are per column, not per file. A clinical table mixes them, so there is no single name to pass; units="SI" is refused with the mapping it wants. PhenoAge exists in an SI and a conventional variant that disagree by years, and units= has no default for that reason.
HbA1c in mmol/mol. Laboratories outside the US report HbA1c in IFCC units. Declare "hba1c": "mmol/mol" and it is converted to the NGSP percentage the reference models were fitted in, by the published master equation NGSP = 0.09148 × IFCC + 2.152 (NGSP; Hoelzel et al., Clin Chem 2004;50:166-174, doi:10.1373/clinchem.2003.024802). It is not a ratio, so it applies to HbA1c only.
A cohort measured unlike its reference. KDM and homeostatic dysregulation are fitted on a reference cohort, and fit_kdm/fit_hd record each marker’s distribution there. When a scored cohort leaves it, score() says so (category reference_range): a median outside the reference’s 1st to 99th percentile, which is what a unit mismatch looks like, or many values beyond the reference’s range. The case that matters most is CRP. NHANES III’s assay read nothing below 0.21 mg/dL, and 63.9% of its adults sit at that floor, so a high-sensitivity CRP cohort scored against it has most of its values where the reference has none. fa.models.clinical.censor_to_reference(df, ref) sets values below a reference’s reporting floor to the floor, which is how the reference itself recorded them, and returns how many moved. It only touches markers whose minimum is a floor (at least 1% of reference rows sitting exactly at it); values above the reference’s range are real measurements and are left alone.

title: Loading your data
text:
Olink NPX
Olink exports long: one row per sample per assay. That is detected and pivoted.
from falconage import preprocess as pp

d = pp.read_olink("olink_npx.csv")
INFO    read_olink: olink_npx.csv is Olink's long export (SampleID, Assay, NPX);
        pivoted to 2 sample(s) x 2 assay(s)
FalconData(2 samples x 2 features, proteomics, olink, 0.0% missing)
A wide matrix of samples by assays is read as it stands. Values stay in NPX, which is already log2 and is the scale the coefficients were fitted in.
For SomaScan, pp.read_somascan() takes RFU and logs it by default, because every published SomaScan aging model here was fitted on logged RFU and feeding it linear values is an order-of-magnitude error that looks like a plausible number.

title: Loading your data
text:
NMR metabolomics
A Nightingale Health export (CSV, TSV or Excel), samples down the rows:
d = fa.read_nightingale("nightingale.xlsx")      # Excel needs the `metabolomics` extra (openpyxl)
res = fa.score(d, clocks=["metaboage", "metabohealth"])
Column names are translated to the BBMRI-NL names the two scores were fitted with, by MiMIR’s table and MiMIR’s rule (lower-cased, and translated only when exactly one entry lists the name); a name the table does not know is kept and listed in obs.attrs["untranslated"] rather than guessed. MetaboAge (van den Akker et al. 2020) and MetaboHealth (Deelen et al. 2019) are scored as MiMIR scores them, its quality control included, and match it to 1e-9 and 1e-12. MetaboHealth z-scores each measure within the cohort, so a score depends on who else is in the file: it is marked requires_cohort and is not comparable between files scored separately.

title: Loading your data
text:
Bulk RNA-seq counts
Genes down the rows, samples across, raw counts rather than TPM.
d = pp.read_counts("counts.csv")
d = pp.prepare_transcriptomic(d)   # RLE, log10, per-sample z, YuGene
FalconData(2 samples x 3 features, transcriptomics, 0.0% missing)
The preparation chain ships and is tested. No transcriptomic clock has a registry entry yet: tAge’s models are licence-restricted, which is a rights problem rather than a technical one, and the chain is here so that supplying one is all that stands between you and a score.

title: Loading your data
text:
After loading
Whatever you loaded, the rest is the same:
res = fa.score(d, clocks="compatible")   # only the clocks this data supports
res.interpretation()                     # scale, unit, legal operations, caveats
fa.technical_se(res, d)                  # how much of each score is the assay
clocks="compatible" is the safe default: it asks the registry which clocks this platform, modality and specimen actually support, and skips the rest by name rather than scoring them on whatever features happen to match.

title: Preprocessing, imputation and coverage
text:
Rows = samples, columns = features. This is the pyaging convention and it should be the new tool’s too. Feature names must be the exact identifiers the clock coefficients use: cg00000029 for human methylation, Ensembl or Entrez for expression, UniProt/Olink assay names for proteins.
pyaging wraps this in AnnData: adata.X is the feature matrix, adata.obs holds sample metadata and later the predictions, adata.uns holds per-clock metadata and missingness diagnostics, adata.obsm["X_<clock>"] is the transient per-clock feature slice (pyaging _pred.py).



EPIC v2 column names look like cg00000029_TC21. Split on _, group by CpG prefix, and average duplicated probes before anything else (pyaging epicv2_probe_aggregation). Skipping this means every EPIC v2 clock silently sees zero overlapping features.



Stage 1 - dataset-level, before the clock. df_to_adata(imputer_strategy=...) with mean, median, constant (0), or knn (default). KNN is expensive on wide matrices and is the first thing to move to GPU.
Stage 2 - clock-level, for features the dataset does not contain at all. pyaging preallocates the clock’s feature matrix, fills present features by index lookup, and fills absent features with the model’s reference_values (typically the training-set mean or a gold-standard median) or with zero if no reference vector was shipped (pyaging check_features_in_adata). It records adata.uns["<clock>_percent_na"] and adata.uns["<clock>_missing_features"], and raises if 100% of features are missing.
Filling with zero in β space means “fully unmethylated”, which is biologically wrong for most sites, always ship a reference vector.
Third stage in tAge: pad missing genes with NA and let the model’s own sklearn SimpleImputer insert training medians. This is the cleanest of the three because the imputation statistic travels with the model.
What FALCONAge does, and what the R packages do. For a linear clock FALCONAge fills an absent feature with the mean of the clock’s observed features over the whole dataset: one constant, the same for every absent feature and every sample (models/linear.py). imputation="reference" replaces it with a per-feature value wherever a reference is supplied. The mitotic mean, percentile and transmission clocks (epiTOC1/2/3, HypoClock, EPICmitHyper/Hypo, stemTOC, stemTOCvitro) are the exception: their published statistic is taken over the sites present, so FALCONAge leaves absent sites out and records imputation: "excluded". methylclock 1.16.0 leaves absent CpGs out of the sum (predAge in R/internals.R), which is a fill of 0. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 fills each one with its per-probe mean from the package’s golden_ref table (meanImputation, called from methyAge). Each policy adds the same amount to every sample, so on one dataset the packages differ by a constant
Δ = Σ_{j absent} w_j (f_j − g_j)
where w_j is the coefficient and f_j, g_j are the two fills. For Horvath’s clocks the constant is multiplied by 21 above the adult age of 20, where the anti-log transform is linear.
Measured on 858 EPIC v1 whole-blood samples from one cohort, on QC-filtered betas, FALCONAge minus each package:

With the absent CpGs filled as the other package fills them, FALCONAge reproduces every sample’s score from each package it was compared with, to four decimal places. The coefficients and intercepts agree (DNAm PhenoAge’s 60.664 is in all three), and the whole offset is the fill. The same betas can therefore put Hannum ages 13 years apart in two established packages with no disagreement about the clock. The offsets belong to a dataset’s missing CpGs, not to the clocks, so the registry does not carry them as per-clock discrepancies. The coverage record (res.coverage[clock_id]) gives the number of values filled (n_imputed) and the method (imputation). Neither 0 nor a pooled mean is a published value for a CpG, which is why a per-CpG reference from each clock’s own training data is the better fill.
Horvath’s normalisation is optional in his own code, and the packages default differently. Horvath 2013 supplied a calibration step (Additional file 24, BMIQcalibration): each sample’s betas over 21,368 probes are mapped onto the distribution of goldstandard2, the per-probe means in Additional file 22 (Genome Biology, CC BY 2.0), after absent probes are set to those means. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 runs it by default for HorvathS2013 (simple_mode = TRUE skips it), methylclock 1.16.0 does not (normalize = FALSE), and FALCONAge offers it as an opt-in step, fa.preprocess.horvath_normalise() (R: horvath_normalise()). Run unmodified on 120 of the same EPIC v1 blood samples, it lowered Horvath 2013 age by a mean 1.87 years (SD 1.15 across samples, −4.6 to +3.3) and left the correlation with chronological age at 0.89; raw and normalised ages correlated at 0.9993. The step moves the level and barely the ranking, so a comparison across packages has to say whether it ran.
horvath_normalise() is a port of BMIQcalibration. The R code fits its beta mixtures on 20,000 probes drawn by set.seed(1); sample(...) and stops its optimisers early (Nelder-Mead after 50 evaluations), so its result depends on the exact draw and the exact optimiser path; the port reproduces each piece as R computes it (the Mersenne-Twister draw, optim’s Nelder-Mead and BFGS, RPMM’s blc, density()). Against the unmodified Additional file 24 it agrees to 3e-10 in beta on a synthetic fixture and to 2e-8 years of Horvath age on the 120 samples above, reproducing the −1.87-year shift. Two arguments follow the code people actually ran:








Argument
Default

title: Preprocessing, imputation and coverage
text:
Rows = samples, columns = features. This is the pyaging convention and it should be the new tool’s too. Feature names must be the exact identifiers the clock coefficients use: cg00000029 for human methylation, Ensembl or Entrez for expression, UniProt/Olink assay names for proteins.
pyaging wraps this in AnnData: adata.X is the feature matrix, adata.obs holds sample metadata and later the predictions, adata.uns holds per-clock metadata and missingness diagnostics, adata.obsm["X_<clock>"] is the transient per-clock feature slice (pyaging _pred.py).



EPIC v2 column names look like cg00000029_TC21. Split on _, group by CpG prefix, and average duplicated probes before anything else (pyaging epicv2_probe_aggregation). Skipping this means every EPIC v2 clock silently sees zero overlapping features.



Stage 1 - dataset-level, before the clock. df_to_adata(imputer_strategy=...) with mean, median, constant (0), or knn (default). KNN is expensive on wide matrices and is the first thing to move to GPU.
Stage 2 - clock-level, for features the dataset does not contain at all. pyaging preallocates the clock’s feature matrix, fills present features by index lookup, and fills absent features with the model’s reference_values (typically the training-set mean or a gold-standard median) or with zero if no reference vector was shipped (pyaging check_features_in_adata). It records adata.uns["<clock>_percent_na"] and adata.uns["<clock>_missing_features"], and raises if 100% of features are missing.
Filling with zero in β space means “fully unmethylated”, which is biologically wrong for most sites, always ship a reference vector.
Third stage in tAge: pad missing genes with NA and let the model’s own sklearn SimpleImputer insert training medians. This is the cleanest of the three because the imputation statistic travels with the model.
What FALCONAge does, and what the R packages do. For a linear clock FALCONAge fills an absent feature with the mean of the clock’s observed features over the whole dataset: one constant, the same for every absent feature and every sample (models/linear.py). imputation="reference" replaces it with a per-feature value wherever a reference is supplied. The mitotic mean, percentile and transmission clocks (epiTOC1/2/3, HypoClock, EPICmitHyper/Hypo, stemTOC, stemTOCvitro) are the exception: their published statistic is taken over the sites present, so FALCONAge leaves absent sites out and records imputation: "excluded". methylclock 1.16.0 leaves absent CpGs out of the sum (predAge in R/internals.R), which is a fill of 0. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 fills each one with its per-probe mean from the package’s golden_ref table (meanImputation, called from methyAge). Each policy adds the same amount to every sample, so on one dataset the packages differ by a constant
Δ = Σ_{j absent} w_j (f_j − g_j)
where w_j is the coefficient and f_j, g_j are the two fills. For Horvath’s clocks the constant is multiplied by 21 above the adult age of 20, where the anti-log transform is linear.
Measured on 858 EPIC v1 whole-blood samples from one cohort, on QC-filtered betas, FALCONAge minus each package:

With the absent CpGs filled as the other package fills them, FALCONAge reproduces every sample’s score from each package it was compared with, to four decimal places. The coefficients and intercepts agree (DNAm PhenoAge’s 60.664 is in all three), and the whole offset is the fill. The same betas can therefore put Hannum ages 13 years apart in two established packages with no disagreement about the clock. The offsets belong to a dataset’s missing CpGs, not to the clocks, so the registry does not carry them as per-clock discrepancies. The coverage record (res.coverage[clock_id]) gives the number of values filled (n_imputed) and the method (imputation). Neither 0 nor a pooled mean is a published value for a CpG, which is why a per-CpG reference from each clock’s own training data is the better fill.
Horvath’s normalisation is optional in his own code, and the packages default differently. Horvath 2013 supplied a calibration step (Additional file 24, BMIQcalibration): each sample’s betas over 21,368 probes are mapped onto the distribution of goldstandard2, the per-probe means in Additional file 22 (Genome Biology, CC BY 2.0), after absent probes are set to those means. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 runs it by default for HorvathS2013 (simple_mode = TRUE skips it), methylclock 1.16.0 does not (normalize = FALSE), and FALCONAge offers it as an opt-in step, fa.preprocess.horvath_normalise() (R: horvath_normalise()). Run unmodified on 120 of the same EPIC v1 blood samples, it lowered Horvath 2013 age by a mean 1.87 years (SD 1.15 across samples, −4.6 to +3.3) and left the correlation with chronological age at 0.89; raw and normalised ages correlated at 0.9993. The step moves the level and barely the ranking, so a comparison across packages has to say whether it ran.
horvath_normalise() is a port of BMIQcalibration. The R code fits its beta mixtures on 20,000 probes drawn by set.seed(1); sample(...) and stops its optimisers early (Nelder-Mead after 50 evaluations), so its result depends on the exact draw and the exact optimiser path; the port reproduces each piece as R computes it (the Mersenne-Twister draw, optim’s Nelder-Mead and BFGS, RPMM’s blc, density()). Against the unmodified Additional file 24 it agrees to 3e-10 in beta on a synthetic fixture and to 2e-8 years of Horvath age on the 120 samples above, reproducing the −1.87-year shift. text:
Platform coverage
Worth running once on an array you have not used before. It reports, per clock, how many features are present and how much of the model’s weight they carry. Two different numbers, and the second is the one that catches EPIC v2 probe loss:

PythonR


fa.probe_loss(d, clocks="scoreable")


probe_loss(d, clocks = "scoreable")




                   tier  n_features  n_present  coverage  mass_coverage  bias_years          heaviest_absent
horvath2013     bundled         353        339    0.9603         0.9715     -1.2570   cg11932564 (0.8%), ...
hannum          bundled          71         64    0.9014         0.8994      1.0279   cg21139312 (2.7%), ...
zhangmortality  bundled          10          9    0.9000         0.7687      0.0124  cg08362785 (23.1%), ...

Three rows of the table for the EPIC v2 series in the test corpus (GSE330325). zhangmortality has nine of its ten CpGs, 90% by count, and the one it lacks carries 23% of its weight.
bias_years is filled in when the platform is one the shift has been measured on; see what probe loss costs. NaN there means not measured, never no bias.
A clock at 96% feature coverage and 61% weight coverage has kept nearly all its probes and lost the ones that matter. The scoring floor applies to both measures, so this run would be refused with a message naming the heaviest absent probes rather than returning a confident number.

title: What a score means
section: Training targets, and what a score means
text:
Training targets, and what a score means



Three quantities that all get called “biological age”, and the units that keep them apart


Chronological age is elapsed time, and it is known without measuring anything. Biological age is an estimate of how worn a body is for that elapsed time. Pace of aging is a rate, years of wear per year of calendar time, and it is the only one of the three that a single sample cannot establish on its own: the Dunedin measure was fitted against two decades of repeated biomarker readings. Because the three carry different units, none of them converts into another, which is why a registry entry declares a scale_type and not only a unit.
What a clock’s output means is set by the outcome it was regressed on. Six families are in common use, and they are not variants of one quantity:

Chronological-age clocks (Horvath 2013 [5], Hannum 2013 [4]) are fitted to calendar age. Their error bars are prediction error against a known truth.
Mortality- and morbidity-trained clocks (PhenoAge [8], GrimAge [11]) are fitted to a survival-weighted composite and then rescaled into years. The unit is years; the target was never age.
Pace-of-aging clocks (DunedinPACE [15]) are fitted to the rate of change in organ-system biomarkers tracked longitudinally. Belsky and colleagues draw the distinction directly:

[Pace-of-aging measures capture] the rate of deterioration in system integrity occurring over a fixed time interval, whereas epigenetic clocks estimate the progress of aging up to a cross-section in time.
Belsky et al., eLife 2022

Mitotic clocks (epiTOC2 [20], StemTOC) estimate cumulative stem-cell divisions. The quantity is a count, not elapsed time.
Causality-enriched clocks (CausAge, DamAge, AdaptAge) restrict features to CpGs with Mendelian-randomisation support, separating damaging from adaptive change (Ying et al., Nature Aging 2024, [19]).
Deconvolution models return cell-type proportions, a composition that is not forced to sum to one; the sum shows how much of the sample the reference explains.

Reporting all six as “biological age” discards the information needed to interpret any of them.

title: What a score means
text:
Scale types and permitted operations



Six of the nine scales, and the four operations most often applied to them without checking


Reading down the acceleration column is the shortest statement of the problem. Only an age in years with a fixed origin admits it. A pace is already a rate, a division count is not elapsed time, and a log hazard is not even on an additive scale, so subtracting a chronological age from any of them produces a number with no units behind it. The matrix drawn here is the same one the code enforces, in LEGAL_OPS.
Every registry entry declares a scale_type alongside its unit, platform, species and the tissue its coefficients were fitted in. That field decides which downstream operations FALCONAge will perform:

Age acceleration is the residual of predicted age on chronological age. It is defined when the prediction is in years and undefined when it is a rate, so asking for it on DunedinPACE is an error with a message, not a number:
IllegalOperationError: 'acceleration' is not defined for dunedinpace, whose output is
pace_ratio (biological years per chronological year).

  A pace of aging is already a rate; subtracting chronological age from it is a units

title: What a score means
text:
8. Output types and units
A tool that returns a bare number is dangerous. Every prediction needs at least six attached fields.

8.1 The output record
res.long() returns one row per sample per clock:
sample_id, clock, value, unit, scale_type, generation, predicts, n_features,
coverage, mass_coverage, n_imputed, availability, registry_version, falconage_version
Acceleration is computed separately (fa.acceleration, with the convention recorded), the missing features and the fill used are in res.coverage, and the coefficient files’ SHA-256, the device and the package versions are in res.manifest. pyaging writes the value into adata.obs[clock] and its metadata and missingness into adata.uns.


8.2 Scale types and what you may do with them

A clock in physical units can be checked against the range its source paper reports, and a median far outside that range is a computation error rather than an unusual cohort. FALCONAge warns (category implausible) when a cohort’s median leaves the interval. For DNAmTL the interval is 4 to 12 kb: Lu et al. 2019 (Table 2) fit DNAmTL = 8.05 − 0.018 × age kb in their test cohorts, 6.2 to 8.0 kb from birth to 100 years. The guard exists because FALCONAge 1.0.0 shipped DNAmTL with its intercept’s sign reversed and returned about −8.5 kb on adult blood; nothing flagged it. Two more human scales carry an interval, each from a published fact about people:



Scale, unit
Interval
Why




age_years, years
−1 to 122.45
No verified human age exceeds Jeanne Calment’s 122 years and 164 days (Robine et al. 2019); an age below −1 year precedes conception


pace_ratio, years per year
0.40 to 2.44
The slowest and fastest members of the Dunedin Study aged 0.40 and 2.44 biological years per chronological year over two decades (Belsky et al. 2022)



The intervals are wide on purpose: they catch a sign, unit or fill error, not an unusual cohort. The pace interval did so on its first real run. Forced below its 80% coverage floor on one cohort’s EPIC v1 betas, DunedinPoAm38 lost 11 of its 46 CpGs, 23% of its weight, and with those filled by the dataset’s mean its median was 0.38. The authors’ own PoAmProjector fills an absent probe with its Dunedin cohort mean, which gives 0.85 on the same data. FALCONAge now fills from those means too.


8.3 Aggregate outputs
FALCONAge returns the first, second and last of these; the composite score and the per-system profile are not built.

Per-sample × per-clock long table (res.long()) and wide matrix (res.wide()).
Age-acceleration matrix, absolute and residual (fa.acceleration(res, method="both")).
Composite score: z-score each clock within cohort, then average within generation class, and report the classes separately rather than mixing generations.
Per-system / per-organ profile (SystemsAge, organAging, tAge tissue clocks) with a radar or heatmap layout.
QC block: missingness per clock, platform detected, imputation used, warnings.

text:

models.NeuralClock(clock, weights, scale=None, notes=list(), reference=None)
A feed-forward network over a fixed probe set.
Forward pass only. Nothing here trains, and the architecture is deliberately the plainest one that fits published aging networks: dense layers, one activation, no dropout at inference, no batch norm state to get wrong.
THE ONE ARCHITECTURE HERE WHERE A GPU EARNS ITS TRANSFER. A linear clock is a single dot product over a few thousand features, and docs/dev/gpu.qmd measures the card losing to the CPU on those by up to 4.6x because moving the matrix costs more than multiplying it. A network is a chain of dense layers with real depth: AltumAge is 20,318 inputs, so the arithmetic per byte transferred is an order of magnitude higher and the transfer amortises. The whole pass therefore runs through the xp handle, activations included, and honours device= like the linear path does.

    result,

Age acceleration, in whichever convention you mean.











Name
Type
Description
Default




adjust
str | Sequence[str] | None
Extra covariates to regress out alongside chronological age. "cell_composition" Use the deconvolution clocks scored in this same run. An acceleration adjusted this way answers “is this person’s blood aging faster”, where the unadjusted version answers “is this person’s blood aging faster or is its cell mix different”, and reports both as one number. a sequence of column names Columns of result.obs, for measured counts or anything else. Only available with method="residual": the absolute convention has no regression to add terms to, and within_group fits per stratum where a composition term would usually be rank-deficient.
None


method
str
"absolute" predicted - chronological. Interpretable in years, and confounded by the clock’s own bias: a clock that over-predicts everyone by three years gives everyone three years of acceleration. "residual" The residual from regressing predicted on chronological age. Centred at zero by construction, which removes that bias and also removes any real cohort-wide effect. The field’s default. "both" Absolute and residual side by side, two columns per clock named <clock>_absolute and <clock>_residual. Suffixed rather than stacked, because the two disagree by several years and a reader who cannot tell which column is which is worse off than with one. "within_group" Residual from a regression fitted separately within each level of group. What the AA2 benchmark needs: it asks whether cases accelerate relative to their own controls, not relative to a line fitted through both. "reference" Residual from a line fitted in another population, reference, and applied unchanged to this one: score - (a + b * age) with a and b estimated on the reference only, separately within each level of the categorical match columns. It answers “how does this person compare with people of the same age and sex in the reference”, which the within-cohort residual cannot, because that residual is centred on this cohort and so absorbs any effect the whole cohort shares.
'residual'


reference

For method="reference": a scored :class:~falconage.score.FalconResult for the reference population, scored with the same fitted model (for KDM, the same fitted :class:~falconage.models.clinical.KDMReference passed to :func:~falconage.score.score for both). It must carry every clock asked for and every match column in its obs.
None


match
Sequence[str]
For method="reference": the obs columns the comparison is matched on. age_col must be one of them; it is the regressor. Every other entry (usually "sex") is categorical, and the line is fitted separately within each of its levels. Levels are compared as text, ignoring case and a trailing .0, so "F" matches "f" but not "female" or 2: recode one side first.
('age', 'sex')














Name
Type
Description





IllegalOperationError
When a clock’s scale does not admit the convention asked for. "absolute", "both" and "reference" need the scale to admit acceleration, because each compares this cohort’s scores with a zero point set somewhere else.



AnalysisError
With method="reference": no reference given, a clock or a match column absent from it, a level of a match column in this result that the reference lacks, fewer than three usable reference samples in a stratum, or a study age outside the ages the reference covers in that stratum (the range is reported; the line is never extrapolated).






Which one a paper used is often not stated, and they disagree by several years on the same data. The convention is recorded in the returned frame’s method attribute so a downstream reader does not have to guess.
WHY A REFERENCE POPULATION. A clock fitted by regression regresses toward the mean age of its training population: it over-predicts the young and under-predicts the old, and a KDM projected from a reference inherits the same pull. In an older cohort predicted - chronological is then negative for most people whatever their health, and the within-cohort residual removes that bias only by centring the cohort on itself. Brain-age work documents the same bias (Smith et al. 2019, NeuroImage 200:528-539, doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.06.017) and corrects it with a regression of the prediction on age whose parameters can be estimated in a training or reference sample and applied unchanged to new data (de Lange and Cole 2020, NeuroImage: Clinical 26:102229, doi:10.1016/j.nicl.2020.102229). "reference" is that regression, fitted in the reference and taken as a residual so that it is on the same footing as "residual" above.
With method="reference" the frame’s attrs["reference_fit"] lists, per clock and stratum, the reference sample size, its age range, the fitted intercept and slope and the residual SD, so the comparison can be audited without the reference in hand.

title: score
text:
score
The scoring loop and its result object.





Name
Description




FalconResult
Scores plus everything needed to say where they came from.





score.FalconResult(
    scores,
    obs,
    manifest,
    registry,
    coverage=dict(),
    skipped=dict(),
    se=None,
)
Scores plus everything needed to say where they came from.
scores is samples x clocks. Everything else – coverage, warnings, weight digests, the resolved config – hangs off the manifest, so a result written to disk and read back is self-describing.





Name
Description




evidence
Published effect sizes for the clocks in this result.


interpretation
One row per clock: what the number is, and what may be done with it.


long
One row per sample per clock, with the scale and provenance attached.





score.FalconResult.evidence(clock=None)
Published effect sizes for the clocks in this result.
The step between a number and something a reader can act on. See :func:falconage.registry.evidence; every row carries its DOI.



score.FalconResult.interpretation()
One row per clock: what the number is, and what may be done with it.
Everything needed to read a score, in the object holding the score. Scale and unit say what the quantity is; legal_operations says which arithmetic the package will perform on it; reliability says how much of a within-person change is likely to be the assay; caveats carries any documented disagreement between the clock’s paper and the coefficients that circulate for it.



score.FalconResult.long()
One row per sample per clock, with the scale and provenance attached.
The scale column is not decoration: it is what stops a reader averaging a mortality log-hazard with an age in years because both were numbers in a column called value.









Name
Description




combine
Stack per-dataset results into one, for a benchmark across studies.


score
Score a dataset against one or more clocks.





score.combine(results, *, keys=None, dataset_col='dataset')
Stack per-dataset results into one, for a benchmark across studies.
Datasets are scored separately and combined afterwards, never merged before scoring. Two reasons, and the second is the one that bites:

a 27K study and an EPIC study have different probe spaces, and the outer join of ten of them is a mostly-NaN matrix that no clock should see;
feature coverage is a property of a dataset. Merged, a clock that covers 99% of one study and 40% of another reports a single meaningless average, and the AA2 test silently compares cases in the well-covered study against controls in the badly-covered one.

Per-clock coverage is kept per dataset in uns and the manifests are merged, so a combined result still says which study contributed what.



score.score(
    data,
    clocks='compatible',
    *,
    device='auto',
    dtype=None,
    imputation='reference',
    min_coverage=0.8,
    reference=None,
    registry=None,
    caller='python',
)
Score a dataset against one or more clocks.











Name
Type
Description
Default




clocks
str | Sequence[str]
"compatible" scores everything this dataset can support and reports the rest as skipped with a reason. "all" attempts every clock of the right modality and fails loudly on the ones that cannot run. A list names them explicitly, and every name in it must work – an explicit request is never silently dropped.
'compatible'


imputation
str
Passed to the per-clock feature alignment. See :func:falconage.models.linear.align; the short version is that zero is never a fill value. The mitotic mean, percentile and transmission clocks ignore it: their published statistic is taken over the features present, so absent ones are left out and the coverage record reads "excluded".
'reference'


min_coverage
float
The fraction of a clock’s features that must be present. Below it, the clock is skipped (clocks="compatible") or raises (explicit list).
0.8


reference

A fitted :class:~falconage.models.clinical.KDMReference or :class:~falconage.models.clinical.HDReference, for the two clinical clocks that have no fixed coefficients.
None

text:
plot.bland_altman
plot.bland_altman(result, clock, *, age_col='age')
Difference against mean, with bias and 95% limits of agreement.
A correlation coefficient cannot show that a clock’s error depends on age. This can, and age-dependent error is the failure mode that makes a single MedAE meaningless: a clock accurate at 40 and eight years out at 80 reports the same summary statistic as one uniformly four years out.

title: preprocess.load_manifest
text:
preprocess.load_manifest

Address-to-probe mapping for one platform, indexed by probe id.
Columns: address_a, address_b (nullable), type (I/II) and channel (Grn/Red, empty for type II). Cached for the process – parsing 850,000 rows per call would dominate a run.
Type II probes have no address_b and no channel: they read methylated in green and unmethylated in red at a single address. Type I probes have two addresses in one channel, and the other channel at those same addresses is the out-of-band signal that :mod:falconage.preprocess.idat uses as its background null.

title: icc
text:
icc
icc(values, subject_col, value_col)
ICC(2,1): two-way random effects, absolute agreement, single measure.
The variant matters and papers rarely say which they used. ICC(2,1) is the one that answers “would a repeat measurement of this person give the same number”, which is the question a clock’s technical reliability is about. ICC(3,1) assumes the raters are the only ones of interest and reports a higher number for the same data.
